items.title: @karpathy：Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now les
items.abstract_or_text: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The funnel is driven by ambition, jaggedness of capability, and access.

items.title: @MiaAI_lab：I've been building something new for TensorFold. It's not just another quant. It's a quantization framework designed aro
items.abstract_or_text: I've been building something new for TensorFold. It's not just another quant. It's a quantization framework designed around how TensorFold actually runs models. I'm calling it Engine-Aware Quantization, or EAQ. First target: GLM 5.3 Flash. Early results vs my current public quant on the same TensorFold version, measured against the original BF16 model: - 41% lower error on what the model actually writes - 54% lower error on the decisions that matter for agents: when to call a tool, which one, when to stop - roughly the same speed.

items.abstract_or_text: AI solved open mathematical problems. But the biggest surprise came afterwards. A team at Google DeepMind has used AI to resolve 9 open Erdos problems, including questions that had remained unsolved for 56 years. The system also proved 44 previously open conjectures about integer sequences. Tsoukalas and coauthors built an agent that generates mathematical proofs in Lean. Paper: Tsoukalas et al., Science (2026)

items.abstract_or_text: The development of AlphaProof was also inspired by the efforts of the formal mathematics community - pioneers like Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London, and the amazing mathematicians that built Lean's Mathlib (and later CSLib). Formal systems like Lean make AI proofs trustworthy, which is why the community's work matters so much today. To add to this community, we started Formal Conjectures, an open repository of precisely stated open problems in Lean built with the community.
